name: Wei Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays I work for Kessler Industrial, a regional contractor that builds warehouses and distribution sheds out by the motorway junction. The steel frame goes up first, then my crew does everything timber inside: the mezzanine floors, the office pods, the stairs, the loading bay doors. Right now it's a big cold-storage warehouse for a food company, and it's huge, you could fit a football pitch inside twice. At weekends I build garden offices with my son-in-law Emre, that's our own little business.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did the garden office business start, and where does technology come in?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: During the years everyone worked from home, a neighbour asked me to build him a shed he could work in, and then his friends asked, and Emre said, let's do this properly. I use AI every day: it draws the garden office designs from the customer's sketch, works out the timber list, writes the quotes, even answers the emails at night. On Kessler sites I use it to check drawings and plan the crew's week. My wife Elif runs the books for the garden offices, and with our savings and the house paid off, we're comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, use it or don't, your choice. Some people will save time, some won't bother. I wouldn't make a big deal of it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means I keep doing what I'm doing. Kessler pays well, the garden offices bring in a bit more, and I've got the AI doing the boring bits already. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working at Kessler until sixty-two or so, keep growing the garden offices with Emre. Maybe do twelve a year instead of eight, since the AI makes the quoting quicker. Then hand the business to Emre when I stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Business as usual, which is good business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much time does the AI save on the garden offices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before, a quote took me a whole evening, drawings, timber list, prices. Now it's twenty minutes, and the customer gets a nice picture of the office in their garden. We win more jobs because we answer first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a downside, for you, in a world where it stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe the competition catches up, because everyone gets the same tools. Then you compete on quality, and I'm happy to do that.

S0.say: I'd say it's a good tool, use it or don't, your choice. I wouldn't make a big deal of it online.
S0.think: It means I keep doing what I do, with good pay at Kessler, extra from the garden offices and AI already doing the boring bits. Fine by me.
S0.do: Keeps working at Kessler Industrial until about sixty-two and grows the weekend garden office business from eight to twelve jobs a year. Plans to hand the business to his son-in-law when he stops.
S0.quote: We win more jobs because we answer first.
S0.fieldNote: Wei is a natural small businessman who already uses AI to win work on his weekend business. He sees AI as a competitive edge and accepts that others will catch up. His family is woven into the business, with his wife on the books and son-in-law as partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Next scenario. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is normal, every generation has its change, and the ones who move first do best. Nobody owes you a job, you make yourself useful. I'd tell the young guys on my crew to learn everything they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is good for me. Steady change means more customers who want things done fast and cheaper, and I'm already ahead. The garden office business could really grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd buy a CNC machine, that's a computer-controlled saw that cuts every piece to the drawing, for about forty thousand from our savings. Then Emre and I could make garden office kits in the workshop and put them up in two days. I'd keep the Kessler job for the steady pay while we grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. Like I've been waiting for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Forty thousand is a big bet. What did Elif say when you raised it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She said, show me the numbers, so I did. If we sell fifteen kits a year it pays for itself in two years. She said yes on the condition the house is never part of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would struggle on your Kessler crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, who's fifty-four and won't use a phone for anything but calls. He's a good worker, but if the measuring and planning go digital, he'll get left. I'd try to help him, but at some point a man has to help himself.

S1.say: I'd say this is normal, every generation has change and those who move first do best. Nobody owes you a job, you make yourself useful.
S1.think: This is good for me, because I'm already ahead and steady change means more customers wanting things fast and cheap. The garden office business could really grow.
S1.do: Buys a computer-controlled saw for about forty thousand from savings to make garden office kits with his son-in-law. Keeps the Kessler job for steady pay while the business grows.
S1.feel: Excited, as if he's been waiting for this.
S1.quote: I'd try to help him, but at some point a man has to help himself.
S1.fieldNote: Wei treats steady change as a business opportunity and has already run the numbers with his wife. His free-market view shows in how he talks about colleagues who don't adapt. He keeps the house off the table, which shows a careful streak under the risk-taking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't wait for the government to save you, get moving. Families should stick together and help each other through. I'd say the government's job is to get out of the way of people trying to adapt, not hand out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years is too fast even for me. If robots can build a garden office, then any big company can make them cheaper than Emre and me. I'd be fine for money, but I'd worry about Emre, he's thirty-five with two little ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd leave Kessler and go full time on the garden offices, to grab as much business as possible before it changes. I'd buy whatever robot or machine lets two people do the work of six, even if it costs a lot of our savings. Once it arrives, if the big companies took over, I'd sell the business while it still had value and give Emre a share to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for myself, but for Emre and my grandkids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Emre, the night you decided to go full time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him, we've got two years to build something worth selling. Every customer, every review, every design we make is value. And if it all falls apart, the family's still here, nobody starves in this family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd say don't wait for the government. Would you accept help from it if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was help for small businesses to buy machines, maybe, yes, that's an investment. A cheque to sit at home, no. I'd rather spend my savings than take that.

S2.say: I'd say don't wait for government to save you, get moving and stick together as families. Government should get out of the way of people adapting, not hand out money.
S2.think: Two years is too fast even for me, because big companies could make garden offices cheaper with robots. I'm fine for money but worry about Emre with two small kids.
S2.do: Leaves Kessler to go full time on the garden offices and buys machines that let two people do six people's work, even at a big cost. Sells the business while it has value if big firms take over, and gives his son-in-law a share to restart.
S2.feel: Uneasy, not for himself but for his son-in-law and grandchildren.
S2.quote: Every customer, every review, every design we make is value.
S2.fieldNote: Wei moves fast even in the hardest scenario, quitting his job to build a sellable business. His unease is about his son-in-law's young family. He separates help to invest, which he'd accept, from cash for staying home, which he refuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same end point, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty of time if you start today. Learn the tools, build something, don't sit and wait. Same message as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one I like. Five years is long enough to grow the garden offices, make the kits, and sell or hand over at the right time. I'd be sixty-three, the perfect age to step back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, buy the CNC saw and start the kits. Year two, leave Kessler and go full time. By year four I'd decide with Emre whether to keep it, add robots, or sell to a bigger firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit fired up. It's a good plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why leave Kessler in year two and not straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Kessler's steady money pays for the machine while we learn. Leave too early and you're spending savings on mistakes. Leave too late and someone else gets the customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about it worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm too sure of myself, maybe. Elif says I always think the next thing will work. Usually it does, but not always.

S3.say: I'd say five years is plenty if you start today. Learn the tools, build something, and don't sit and wait.
S3.think: This one I like, there's time to grow the garden offices and sell or hand over at sixty-three, the perfect age to step back.
S3.do: Buys the computer-controlled saw and starts making kits in year one, then leaves Kessler for the business in year two. By year four decides with his son-in-law whether to add robots, keep it or sell.
S3.feel: Calm and fired up by a good plan.
S3.quote: Leave too early and you're spending savings on mistakes. Leave too late and someone else gets the customers.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits Wei's plans neatly, and he laid out a year-by-year roadmap without hesitation. When asked what worries him, he admitted overconfidence, quoting his wife. Timing is the thing he thinks hardest about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say with ten years nobody has an excuse. If you're young, learn a trade and learn the tools, both. If you're old like me, set up your family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's after I've stepped back. I'd hand the garden offices to Emre at sixty-two and let him decide what to do with the robots. I'd advise from the porch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working at Kessler until sixty-two and grow the garden offices steadily, adding new tools as they come. Then hand the business to Emre with a plan for the robot years. Keep our savings as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, really, it's a good place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that plan for the robot years look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Write down what we know about customers, designs, suppliers, so Emre isn't starting from zero. Tell him when to buy machines and when to wait. That's the most useful thing I can leave him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandkids about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to do something with your hands and with your head. And whatever comes, don't wait for someone to hand you a life. Build it.

S4.say: I'd say with ten years nobody has an excuse. Young people should learn a trade and the tools, and older people should set up their families.
S4.think: It's after I've stepped back, so I'd hand the garden offices to Emre at sixty-two and let him decide about robots. I'd advise from the porch.
S4.do: Works at Kessler until sixty-two while steadily growing the garden office business with new tools. Hands it to his son-in-law with a written plan for the robot years.
S4.feel: Calm and happy, in a good place.
S4.quote: Write down what we know about customers, designs, suppliers, so Emre isn't starting from zero.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year scenario lets Wei think as a family elder passing on a business. His main gift to his son-in-law is knowledge and timing advice. His self-reliant values run through his message to his grandchildren.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to build anything worth handing on. What would help is less red tape for small firms trying to change, and maybe help buying the machines, as a loan, not a gift. And families looking after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask people what they'd build if they had the time. Everyone talks about losing jobs. Some of us see a chance to make something new.

headlineQuote: And whatever comes, don't wait for someone to hand you a life. Build it.
portrait: Wei Yilmaz is a 58-year-old carpenter who fits out warehouse interiors for an industrial contractor on weekdays and builds garden offices with his son-in-law at weekends. A daily AI user with a paid-off house and savings, he already uses AI to design and quote and wins jobs by answering first. He's calm or excited in most scenarios and would invest about forty thousand in a computer-controlled saw if change is steady. The two-year AGI case makes him uneasy for his son-in-law's young family, and he'd quit his job to build a sellable business fast. He believes in self-reliance, family and help to invest rather than handouts.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to build something worth handing on to his family.
whatWouldHelp: Less red tape for small firms trying to change and help buying machines as a loan rather than a gift, plus families looking after each other.
